verdictSummary: MacWhisper's solo core is compact: build a private local transcription pipeline that accepts an audio file, transcribes it, creates structured notes, and exports Markdown. A competent builder can reach a useful personal version in one sitting, while the paid product mainly wins on capture, integrations, reliability.
coreLoopDIY: Build a private local transcription pipeline that accepts an audio file, transcribes it, creates structured notes, and exports Markdown.
replacementScope: personal replacement for the core loop
requirements: local Whisper model or optional API key in .env
whyPeopleStillPay: MacWhisper: Customers pay for automatic capture, dependable speaker handling, search across calls, and notes arriving without manual file wrangling.
ongoingBurden: Own audio capture permissions, diarization quality, model downloads, storage, privacy, and integrations.

priorArt.name: whisper.cpp
priorArt.desc: Local speech-to-text engine suitable for private transcription.

alternatives.name: Buzz
alternatives.desc: MacWhisper’s basic job, minus the Mac-only part and the invoice.

facts.install: Install the desktop package for macOS, Windows, or Linux; package-manager and source installs are also available
facts.engines: Runs local Whisper-family backends including faster-whisper and whisper.cpp-compatible models, and can use the OpenAI transcription API when the user supplies a key.
facts.dataFormat: With a local backend, source media, downloaded model files, job state, and exported TXT/SRT/VTT/CSV transcripts remain on the computer; selecting an API backend sends the audio to that provider under its terms.
facts.gapVsPaid: Buzz covers local transcription and batch export, but it is less Mac-native and has a thinner editor, speaker workflow, automation surface, and system integration than MacWhisper.
facts.setupBlocker: The app installs cleanly, but the first transcription triggers a multi-hundred-megabyte or multi-gigabyte model download and CPU-only transcription can be dramatically slower than real time.

alternatives.name: noScribe
alternatives.desc: A hefty local interview transcriber with speaker labels and an editor; several gigabytes, zero minute meter.

facts.install: Download the large desktop installer/package for the operating system and let the app install or fetch its transcription models
facts.engines: Uses local OpenAI Whisper-family speech recognition through faster-whisper/CTranslate2 and local speaker diarization components; model size and diarization can be selected in the app.
facts.dataFormat: Audio/video, downloaded model weights, transcript projects, speaker labels, edits, and exported text/subtitle files remain on the user's machine; no hosted transcription account is required.
facts.gapVsPaid: noScribe adds diarization and an editor, but its multi-gigabyte footprint, interview-oriented workflow, slower interface, and rougher platform packaging are much less polished than MacWhisper.
facts.setupBlocker: The first obstacle is weight: the application and model downloads consume several gigabytes, and diarization plus large Whisper models can be slow or memory-hungry on ordinary hardware.

alternatives.name: Subtitle Edit
alternatives.desc: A subtitle workbench with Whisper bolted in; ugly enough to be trustworthy, useful enough to stay installed.

facts.install: Windows installer or portable ZIP; Linux/macOS users use the separate cross-platform build and its platform prerequisites
facts.engines: Supports local Whisper engines such as whisper.cpp and faster-whisper/Purfview's Faster-Whisper, plus optional cloud speech-recognition services when configured.
facts.dataFormat: Media, subtitle projects, dictionaries, downloaded speech models, and exported SRT/VTT/ASS and other subtitle formats live on disk; choosing a cloud speech backend sends the relevant audio to that provider.
facts.gapVsPaid: Subtitle Edit is a Windows-first subtitle workshop whose dense interface and separate engine downloads are a poor substitute for MacWhisper's native drag-and-drop transcription experience.
facts.setupBlocker: For a Mac user the first obstacle is that Subtitle Edit is Windows-first, and speech-to-text normally requires an additional engine/model download before the transcription menu becomes useful.

alternatives.name: Vibe
alternatives.desc: A cross-platform desktop transcriber with subtitles, batch jobs, translation and optional local summaries.

facts.install: Install the macOS, Windows, or Linux desktop release
facts.engines: Runs Whisper-family models locally through its native inference stack; optional summarization can be routed to a locally running Ollama model or configured API-backed language-model providers.
facts.dataFormat: Source media, model weights, transcript history, and exported TXT/SRT/VTT/JSON files stay on the computer for local transcription; any optional cloud summarization sends transcript text to the selected provider.
facts.gapVsPaid: Vibe is clean and cross-platform, but its editor, diarization, dictation capture, automation, and Mac-specific workflow integration are less mature than MacWhisper's.
facts.setupBlocker: The first run must download a Whisper model, and users on unsupported or older GPUs may face long jobs, high memory use, or an operating-system security prompt for a community-distributed binary.

notes: Strong page because MacWhisper separates a compact personal workflow from the value of long-term polish.
prompt:
Build a usable personal replacement for the core loop of MacWhisper.
Use exactly this stack: Python 3.12 + FastAPI + whisper.cpp + SQLite.
Primary job: Build a private local transcription pipeline that accepts an audio file, transcribes it, creates structured notes, and exports Markdown.
Start from an empty folder and create the complete working project.
Make the default mode single-user and private.
Store user data locally unless the core job requires the declared self-hosted database.
Do not add analytics, telemetry, ads, or third-party accounts.
Put every secret and external credential in .env and provide .env.example.
Use realistic sample data that is clearly labelled and easy to delete.
Implement the smallest polished interface that completes the core loop end to end.
Include clear empty, loading, validation, success, and failure states.
Add import and export so the user is not trapped in the app.
Use accessible keyboard navigation, labels, focus states, and sensible contrast.
Validate untrusted input and never log secrets or private file contents.
Deliberately exclude these paid-product advantages: cross-call team analytics; meeting-bot auto-join; live multi-speaker accuracy.
Do not fake integrations, network effects, proprietary data, model quality, compliance, or security claims.
Where an external API is optional, keep the app useful without it and explain the degraded mode.
Write focused unit tests for the data model and the most important workflow.
Add one end-to-end smoke test that proves the core loop works.
Create a README with setup, permissions, architecture, data location, backup, and limitations.
Add scripts for install, development, test, build, and a production-style local run.
Run the tests and build before finishing, then fix errors rather than merely describing them.
